touches.text: System: a box has to name itself before any bus is up (a saveslate, an install), so the system device publishes the host's name and OS family (6.6.3.7). - akiendelllinux_cc_0 2.3.8Every device has the panes the base shim defines (17.1.3.5.2), drawn by the web server (15):

Declaring a new instance rotates, explicitly or implicitly: --new rotates explicitly, no flag rotates implicitly, --name overrides both. -amm Reading (superclaude is the rescue service's launcher, cairn/devices/cc/superclaude; none of these needs a folder prepared by hand): - `cairn superclaude --new` always rotates explicitly to the next undeclared n (cc_1 when cc_0 is declared, cc_2 when cc_1 is, and so on), then declares, wires and launches it. - `cairn superclaude` with no flag rotates implicitly: it starts cc_0 when cc_0 is free, and when cc_0 is taken (running) it rotates as --new does. - `cairn superclaude --name <x>` uses exactly x and overrides all of that: it declares x if absent, then launches it. - The declared folder commits through the door in the same act, so the house tree is not left dirty and crossings are not refused. - The one CC inference here: "implicitly" is read as taken (running) cc_0 means rotate, while a declared-but-stopped cc_0 is simply started. Tickets: aa05710a5124 reshapes to this; d13859e2ae46 is the implicit rotation; 0f7a8cada1ca names the next undeclared n. - akiendelllinux_orchestrator
Nothing requires Akien's word for a proof to run. A proof that starts Windows processes runs without asking; no env var or standing flag gates it.
On every Windows box, what Cairn starts runs without a console window by default; a window opens only when someone asks for one. WHY: the boxes serve him (the media box showed pop-ups during videos).
Owned by the Cairn device. Mostly a router.

The launcher walks the words. `cairn cairn foo bar` (the long form) means "tell the cairn device to run foo with argument bar". At each level: is the next word a machine here? Step into it and take the next word. Is it a script in this level's bin/? Run it, pass back the result, done. Neither? It is a bus verb: send it to this level over the bus. So `cairn foo bar baz`: foo is a device; it has a machine bar; bar's bin/ has baz, so baz runs. No bar machine? bar goes to foo over the bus. Each check is one directory lookup, so it is fast. WHY scripts first: scripts are the simple path; the bus is the route to what a device answers itself.

Scripts are Python wherever possible, run by Cairn's own interpreter, so one file works on every platform. Platform-specific ones match their platform: executable or .sh on Linux; .bat, .cmd or .ps1 on Windows.

Repo-root bin/ holds only the launcher itself, the one thing on PATH. Every shortcut lives in the bin/ of the device or machine it belongs to; its bin/ plus its bus verbs is what help lists at that level.
The launcher is Python (bin/cairn), run by Cairn's own interpreter, so Windows needs no bash. Typing `cairn` works on either platform.

In front of it sits a thin platform shell (a shell script on Linux, cairn.cmd or cairn.ps1 on Windows) with enough brains to fall over to Rescue (6.5) when it can't find Cairn's Python, or Python throws, or anything else stops the launcher. The failure throws a trouble ticket (3.4.3), and the ticket is Rescue's "read this" (6.5.3.5); a repeat increments that ticket's counter. Rescue's prompt says: at the end of proving the fix, check for more errors, to clear or fix as appropriate. WHY: trouble has to be able to report when nothing else can (2.3.7.1.3).
With no Python at all, the trouble class can't run, so the shell writes the trouble file itself, in the same format, and finds a matching open one to increment.

Only a failure of the launcher itself falls over to Rescue. A command that runs and fails (eg a verb that exits 1) is that command's error, reported as usual. The Python launcher marks its own failure in a way the shell can tell apart (eg a reserved exit code).

Rescue is interactive, so the shell launches it only when someone is at a terminal. Called from a script, a hook or a schedule, it throws (or increments) the trouble just the same and exits loudly with an error, leaving the ticket for the next Rescue. WHY: nothing may hang waiting on a Claude nobody sees.
Bringing Cairn to a new platform is a Rescue job, done on that platform (eg Windows, from inside an elevated PowerShell). WHY: Claude writes better Windows code on Windows.
On a new platform a simple cairn.bat comes first: at the start it takes only the rescueclaude option, launching Claude with 200K context and dangerous permissions.
Owns the CC launcher (superclaude): starts Claude Code with Cairn's session contract, in its own memory-capped cgroup. WHY: Claude can OOM the box.

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.

Any device or machine may have a bin/ beside its code. That folder IS its list of shortcuts: add a file to add one, delete it to remove one. A shortcut is a script that calls the long form (eg `cairn superclaude` -> `cairn cc superclaude`; `cairn show temp` -> `cairn recovery show temp`), which also saves the walk from searching farther, or does work itself (eg install). Shortcuts live beside what they serve (RULE 1). `cairn foo` whose first word is not a device means `cairn cairn foo`: top-level shortcuts are the cairn device's bin/.

Install and upgrades live here: the installer machine walks the host-seam intentions, verifies each, offers what's missing, applies, re-verifies. If xyz library needs an update, this is the component that does it. Any change to what the host is goes through here (6.6.3.1.1).
Code home: the bootstrap floor that comes up before anything else lives in the Recovery device; superclaude, the CC launcher, lives in the CC device (10).

Owns the Claude Code hooks: mail check, the turn-shape and ask scans, the gates on record writes and deletes. Anything that adapts CC specifically to Cairn goes in the CC device, and every one of CC's scripts lives here.
Instance: every device has at least one; a singleton is instance 0.
The exceptions are client tools a device publishes:

There is no central supervisor. Each part starts what it needs by trying to use it: sending a message starts the bus if it is down, a message arriving wakes its shim, the shim wakes its device. Many very small supervisors, each one detect-and-start. WHY: a supervisor is one more thing to keep up, and the system must come up from any part that is touched.
The detect-and-start lives in one tool, the waker, and it sits inside connect: every client's connect is a wake attempt, so no caller can forget one. A probe watches and reports; the waker acts.

More than one instance of a device is allowed: many things can be singletons or not (eg a second embeddings generator on another host when traffic is heavy). Instances have distinct names so messages route. Naming is the shim's job: the launcher asks the shim for an instance, and a shim given no name when cc_0 exists launches cc_1.
INTENTION:
sudo_relay (machine): Recovery's way to root on Linux, needed for installs and upgrades.
Rescue (Claude Code outside Cairn; part of Recovery, not a device of its own)
Launched automatically by a failed install, start or launch, with "read this" and the trouble ticket saying what happened and what it wants to make happen. The operator can also launch it by hand.

The hostname comes from the system device. It answers which box (the short hostname, lowercased) and which OS family, and nothing else in Cairn asks the OS for the hostname. Callers reach it through the client tool it publishes (2.3.7.1.5), so a box names itself on every OS, Windows included, with no bus running. - akiendelllinux_cc_0
